maps.title: Gauge theory
maps.abstract: A gauge theory is a type of field theory in which the Lagrangian is invariant under certain local transformations. These local transformations are dependent on the spacetime point, and a formally defined in terms of a principal bundle with the gauge group as its fiber. The matter fields carry representations of the gauge group, and formally live in associated vector bundles. The gauge field is a connection on the principal bundle. Common examples include electromagnetism, where the gauge group is `U(1)`, and the Standard Model of particle physics, where the gauge group is `SU(3) × SU(2) × U(1)`.

maps.title: Configuration Space
maps.abstract: The configuration space of a mechanical system is the manifold of its configurations, and its charts are generalised coordinates. It is the base on which the Lagrangian formulation of mechanics is built, Lagrangians being functions on its tangent bundle of positions and velocities. Particular systems, such as the harmonic oscillator and the pendulum, have configuration spaces of their own, which are to be configuration spaces in this general, system-agnostic sense.

maps.title: Damped harmonic oscillator
maps.abstract: A damped harmonic oscillator is a mass under a restoring force proportional to its displacement and a damping force proportional to its velocity, so that m ẍ + γ ẋ + k x = 0. Its data is that of the undamped oscillator — a positive mass and spring constant — together with a nonnegative damping coefficient, and position and velocity live in one-dimensional Euclidean space, with a trajectory a map from time into it. The sign of the discriminant γ² − 4 m k splits the motion into underdamped, critically damped and overdamped regimes, each solved in closed form, and the Caldirola–Kanai Lagrangian gives the dissipative dynamics a variational description.

maps.title: Hamiltonian mechanics
maps.abstract: Hamiltonian mechanics separates the kinematics of a system, described by its phase space, from its dynamics, specified by a Hamiltonian. Hamilton's equations determine the motion, and Poisson brackets describe the evolution of observables. Symmetries give conserved quantities, while Liouville integrability requires sufficiently many independent conserved quantities in involution. The coordinate formulations of the harmonic oscillator, simple pendulum and central-force systems provide examples, alongside a symplectic vector-space formulation of moment maps and conservation.

maps.title: Configuration space of the harmonic oscillator
maps.abstract: The one-dimensional harmonic oscillator is a mass on a spring: one particle on a line, pulled back by a force proportional to its displacement. Its configuration is a single real coordinate, so its configuration space is a one-dimensional smooth manifold, a trajectory is a curve from time into that manifold, and the kinetic energy comes from the mass metric, the mass-scaled Euclidean inner product on tangent vectors. Treated geometrically rather than in coordinates, the configuration space carries a global chart onto the Euclidean model and a map into physical space; smoothness of a trajectory reduces to smoothness of its coordinate curve, the velocity is the derivative of that curve, and the geometric kinetic energy is the familiar mass-scaled expression.

maps.title: Lagrangian mechanics
maps.abstract: A Lagrangian system on a smooth manifold of configurations is a smooth function of time and of the positions and velocities, that is, a function on time and the tangent bundle of the manifold. Its motions are the critical points of the action, the integral of the Lagrangian along a curve, under smooth variations of the curve that fix its endpoints. Around this sit the Euler–Lagrange equations in charts, Noether's theorem with the conservation laws it gives, the conservation of energy for autonomous systems, natural systems built from a Riemannian metric, and Lagrangians written in generalised coordinates.

maps.title: Configuration space for pendulum
maps.abstract: A pendulum is a mass swinging under gravity on a string or a rod. Its configuration is fixed by the angles it makes and, when the support can move, by the position of the support, so its configuration space is naturally a product of circles and lines in the sense of the general configuration space of a mechanical system. This map covers two pendulum problems: the sliding pendulum, whose configuration is the support position together with the string angle, and the simple pendulum, whose configuration is a single angle taken modulo a full turn and whose dynamics are recorded in full separately.

maps.title: Simple pendulum
maps.abstract: A simple pendulum is a bob on a rigid massless rod of length ℓ, pinned at a pivot and swinging in a vertical plane under gravity g. Its configuration is the angle of the rod from the downward vertical, taken modulo a full turn, so the configuration space is a circle and the bob sits at (ℓ sin θ, −ℓ cos θ) in the plane. The motion obeys θ̈ + (g/ℓ) sin θ = 0, which admits Newtonian, Lagrangian and Hamiltonian formulations, conserves energy, and has a unique solution for given initial angle and angular velocity. For small amplitudes the pendulum is a harmonic oscillator of period 2π√(ℓ/g); for librations — amplitudes below the inverted position — the period grows with the amplitude and is given by the complete elliptic integral 4√(ℓ/g) K(sin²(θ₀/2)).

maps.title: Rigid body
maps.abstract: A rigid body in d-dimensional space is specified by its mass distribution, which is what a body contributes to any integral over it: a linear functional on the smooth functions on space. From that single piece of data come the total mass, the centre of mass and the inertia tensor, both about the origin and about an arbitrary point, with the solid sphere as a worked example. A rigid body in motion additionally carries the trajectory of its centre of mass and its orientation at each time, from which come the velocity of the centre of mass, the angular velocity — in any dimension as a skew-symmetric tensor, and in three dimensions as the dual vector obtained by the hat map — and the kinetic energy, which splits into a translational part and a rotational part about the centre of mass (the König decomposition).

maps.title: FLRW cosmology
maps.abstract: A Friedmann–Lemaître–Robertson–Walker spacetime models a universe that is homogeneous and isotropic. Its geometry is fixed by a scale factor, a function of cosmic time on the time manifold, together with the curvature of the spatial slices, which is spherical, flat or saddle. The expansion rate is the Hubble parameter, its change is measured by the deceleration parameter, and the dynamics is governed by the Friedmann equations, which tie the scale factor to the energy density and pressure of the cosmic fluid, to the spatial curvature and to the cosmological constant. Around these sit the continuity equation, barotropic equations of state with their density scaling laws, the cosmological constant as a fluid, exact solutions, the density parameters and their closure relation, the reduced Hubble function of the standard cosmological model, the age of the universe, the energy conditions of the cosmic fluid with the acceleration criterion, eternal expansion together with the Big-Bang bound on the interval of cosmic time, and the cosmological distances, the redshift and the horizons.

maps.title: Electromagnetic Potential
maps.abstract: The electromagnetic potential is the primitive kinematic object of electromagnetism: a map from spacetime to contravariant Lorentz vectors, carrying its own additive-group and scalar-action structure and the action of the Lorentz group, with a distributional counterpart given by a tempered distribution on spacetime valued in Lorentz vectors. It can be built from a scalar potential, from a vector potential, or from a pair of non-relativistic potentials, and recovered from the electric and magnetic fields in the Poincaré gauge; from it come the electric field, the magnetic field, the field-strength term and the electromagnetic Lagrangian, in both the function and the distributional settings.

maps.title: Fluid
maps.abstract: A fluid is described by the spatial distribution of its velocity, density and pressure, as fields over space and time, and the continuity equation, the equations of motion and the thermodynamic balance laws are statements about those fields. The independent data is spread over a tower of structures: a fluid flow carries density and velocity, a Cauchy flow adds the stress tensor and the specific body force, and a thermodynamic Cauchy flow adds entropy and enthalpy, while pressure enters through the stress laws.

maps.title: Lattice QFT
maps.abstract: Lattice quantum field theory regularizes a Euclidean quantum field theory by replacing continuous spacetime with a hypercubic lattice of spacing a, usually periodic so that the lattice is a finite torus, with matter fields on the sites and gauge fields on the oriented links as elements of a compact gauge group. On a finite lattice the Euclidean path integral is an ordinary finite-dimensional integral, Lebesgue measure for scalar fields and Haar measure for link variables, weighted by the exponential of minus the lattice action; the theory is then a genuine probability measure on field configurations whose moments are the correlation functions. The physical questions concern those measures: reflection positivity, the transfer matrix and the mass gap, confinement through Wilson loops, and the behaviour as the spacing goes to zero and the volume to infinity. The gauge-field side builds on gauge theory.

maps.title: Two Higgs Doublet Model
maps.abstract: The two Higgs doublet model extends the Standard Model with a second Higgs doublet, so that a configuration is a pair of Higgs vectors. The global gauge group acts on such pairs, and their gauge orbits are pinned down by the Gram matrix of the pair or, equivalently, by the Gram vector of its components in the Pauli basis; both invariants characterize orbits and are surjective onto the matrices or vectors satisfying the obvious constraints. On top of these sit the potential of the model, its gauge invariance, its expression in terms of the Gram vector, and its stability theory, including an explicit counterexample to a step in one of the references.

maps.title: Standard Model gauge group
maps.abstract: The gauge group of the Standard Model is SU(3) × SU(2) × U(1), but only up to a quotient: a finite central subgroup may be divided out, and which one is not settled by the physics known so far. This area therefore treats both the full group and the group obtained for a given choice of quotient, by the sixth, second or third roots of unity, or by nothing at all, together with the projections onto the three factors, the star structure, the roots of unity as central subgroups, the common quotient map and its kernel, and the U(1) and fundamental SU(2) actions on the two-dimensional complex space of the Higgs sector; the Higgs field builds on this group.

maps.title: Higgs Field
maps.abstract: A Higgs field is a smooth section of the Higgs bundle over spacetime, on which the global Standard Model gauge group acts; for now the bundle is the trivial one, whose fibre is the two-dimensional complex vector space of pointwise Higgs values. The pointwise values carry an orthonormal basis, real scalar coordinates, and a gauge representation whose orbits are classified by the norm, while fields carry constant fields, smooth components, a pointwise inner product and norm squared, the Standard Model Higgs potential with its minimization theory, and invariant effective potentials on pointwise values; the two Higgs doublet model builds on this area.

maps.title: Feynman diagrams
maps.abstract: A Feynman diagram is a partition of a multiset of field operators into disjoint pairs: the multiset counterpart of a Wick contraction, which pairs up positions in a list of field operators. Passing from lists to multisets makes a diagram independent of the order in which the operators are written down, and the resulting many-to-one map from contractions to diagrams is what a symmetry factor accounts for. The area rests on the existing perturbation-theory material: the field specification fixes the fields of a theory, their bosonic or fermionic statistics and the labels from which field operators and their creation and annihilation parts are built; the free operator algebra and the Wick algebra are where the value of a diagram is computed; and Wick contractions supply the pairings of a list with their Koszul signs, time contractions and Wick's theorem. A position field operator carries a point of spacetime, a Lorentz vector acted on by the Lorentz group.

maps.title: Topological field theory
maps.abstract: A topological field theory assigns algebraic data to manifolds in a way that depends only on their topology. In the Atiyah–Segal formulation, a theory in dimension d is a symmetric monoidal functor from a category of cobordisms, whose objects are closed oriented (d−1)-manifolds and whose morphisms are oriented d-dimensional cobordisms between them, to the category of modules over a fixed commutative ring. The state space of a closed (d−1)-manifold is the value of the functor on that object, and the partition function of a closed d-manifold is its value on that manifold read as a cobordism from the empty manifold to itself. No metric on the world-volume enters, so every number and every space produced this way is an invariant of the underlying manifold. The one-dimensional world-volume is the time manifold, which carries an orientation but no metric.

maps.title: Hilbert spaces on Space
maps.abstract: The Hilbert space on space with a given measure is the L² space: the complex functions that are square-integrable against that measure, taken up to equality almost everywhere, with the volume as the default measure. These are the spaces non-relativistic quantum mechanics works in, and they come together with the subspaces singled out by regularity, support and boundary conditions, and with the multiplication and derivative operators that quantum mechanics needs on them.

maps.title: Hilbert space tensor products
maps.abstract: The Hilbert space of a composite quantum system is the tensor product of the Hilbert spaces of its parts. The algebraic tensor product of two Hilbert spaces is an inner-product space but need not be complete, so the right object is its completion, the complete tensor product, taken for a pair of Hilbert spaces and for an indexed family of them, together with the structure maps relating the various ways of bracketing and ordering the factors.

maps.title: Operator algebra
maps.abstract: An observable of a quantum system is a self-adjoint operator on the Hilbert space of states, and the observables of interest are almost never defined on the whole space: position multiplies a wavefunction by a coordinate and momentum differentiates it, and both send square-integrable functions out of the space unless the wavefunction decays or is smooth enough. The objects are therefore partially defined linear maps with a dense domain, together with symmetry of the inner-product pairing on that domain and self-adjointness, which is strictly stronger than symmetry once the domain is a proper subspace. On an arbitrary complex Hilbert space this gives the adjoint calculus, multiplication operators, and the statistics of an observable in a state, culminating in the Robertson and Robertson-Schrödinger uncertainty bounds; on the Hilbert space on space it gives the standard observables of non-relativistic quantum mechanics on space — position, powers of the radius, momentum -iℏ∂ᵢ and angular momentum 𝐋ᵢⱼ = xᵢpⱼ - xⱼpᵢ — with their canonical commutation relations. The spectrum, the resolvent, the numerical range and spectral measures belong to spectral theory instead.

maps.title: Spectral theory of unbounded operators
maps.abstract: The measured values of an observable are the points of the spectrum of the operator representing it, so the spectral theory of an unbounded operator is what connects the formalism to experiment. For partially defined operators on a complex Hilbert space it comprises the resolvent and the resolvent set, the spectrum with its point, residual and continuous parts, the regularity domain with the deficiency subspace and the defect number, the numerical range, and spectral measures. Two results carry the physical content: for a symmetric operator every point off the real axis is a point of regularity, and the defect numbers at i and -i decide essential self-adjointness; for a self-adjoint operator the spectrum is real and the residual spectrum empty, so a measurement returns a real number. The algebraic theory of the operators themselves lives in the operator algebra.

maps.title: QuantumSystem
maps.abstract: A quantum system in non-relativistic quantum mechanics is fixed by two choices: a complex Hilbert space, and a self-adjoint Hamiltonian operator on it. Everything else is built from that pair: the trivial system on the zero-dimensional space, unitary equivalence of systems, the sum of two systems, and the dynamics, namely the Schrödinger equation, the time evolution operator, the energy eigenvalues and eigenbases, and the passage to the Heisenberg picture.

maps.title: Qubits
maps.abstract: A qubit is a two-level quantum system, labelled by the two-element type of its computational basis. A pure state of a qubit is a ket on that type, and a general state is a density matrix on it, both coming from the theory of finite dimensional systems. What is specific to qubits is the standard single-qubit gates, the controlled version of a unitary with a qubit as control, the Bloch sphere with its angular parameterization and the geometric phase of triples of states, and, for pairs and registers of qubits, entanglement and universality.

maps.title: Dirac Fermions
maps.abstract: A Dirac fermion is the four-component spinor built from a left-handed Weyl fermion together with a dual right-handed one: it is a complex vector space with a four-element chiral basis, carrying the representation of SL(2, ℂ) induced from its two Weyl factors, and so of the Lorentz group through its double cover. The gamma endomorphisms act in the chiral basis and satisfy the Clifford relations for the Minkowski signature (+,−,−,−); their chirality operator gives complementary left and right chiral projectors, and a change of coordinates turns them into the concrete gamma matrices of the Dirac representation, which generate the Dirac algebra and realize it as a quotient of the Clifford algebra of the Minkowski quadratic form. This is the setting for the Dirac equation, the Dirac bilinears and the fermionic terms of the Standard Model Lagrangian.

maps.title: Weyl Fermions
maps.abstract: Weyl fermions are the two-component spinors carrying the fundamental representations of SL(2, ℂ), the double cover of the restricted Lorentz group. There are four of them — the left-handed and right-handed Weyl spinors and their duals — each a complex vector space with a two-element basis and a representation of SL(2, ℂ); on top of these sit the invariant contractions pairing each type with its dual, the epsilon metrics that raise and lower spinor indices, the units realizing the duality, and the identification of pairwise tensor products with 2 × 2 matrices. They underlie the Dirac fermions and the fermionic sector of the Standard Model.

maps.title: Lorentz Group
maps.abstract: The Lorentz group is the group of real matrices Λ preserving the Minkowski metric η, those satisfying Λ * dual Λ = 1 where dual Λ = η Λᵀ η. It is the symmetry group of Minkowski spacetime, and is used throughout the library: Lorentz tensors, Weyl and Dirac fermions, and the electromagnetic potential are all characterized by how they transform under it. The group sits as a closed subgroup of the general linear group, contains the boosts and the rotations, admits several equivalent membership conditions, and has distinguished subsets: the proper transformations, the orthochronous ones, and the restricted Lorentz group where both conditions hold.

maps.title: Tensors
maps.abstract: Tensors appear in one form or another throughout physics. The most common example is the Lorentz tensors, which in the most general setting also include Weyl fermions, and are associated with the Lorentz group in the real case and `SL(2, ℂ)` in the complex case. In this API we define the general framework for working with these tensors, and others, and their corresponding indices. The goal is to enable physicists to use index notation in a similar way to how they would on pen and paper.

maps.title: Galilean group
maps.abstract: The Galilean group is the group of transformations relating the descriptions two observers give of non-relativistic space and time. An element records a spatial rotation, a boost velocity, a translation of space and a translation of time, in any spatial dimension; it acts on a pair of an instant and a point by rotating and boosting first, then translating, and it contains the Euclidean group, the orthogonal group, the rotations, the space translations and the time translations as subgroups.

maps.title: Reference frame
maps.abstract: An observer describing motion needs a coordinate grid, and the grid is a choice rather than a feature of space: two points of space determine a displacement, but a displacement acquires numerical components only once axes have been picked, the observer need not use the zero point space carries, and no instant of time is canonically zero. A reference frame is that collection of choices, a time origin together with an origin and a set of axes carried along through time. An inertial frame is one whose grid is not being pushed around, the setting in which the familiar Newtonian statements about free motion hold, and a vector quantity measured by an observer is a list of components read off that observer's axes, whose lengths and angles are nevertheless taken from the underlying space.

maps.title: Space
maps.abstract: A point of space is modelled by its d real coordinates, read against an arbitrary but fixed choice of length unit and origin; the default dimension is three, but nothing is special to it, and the space is flat and Euclidean throughout. Around that bare structure sit the structures physics needs on space: a metric and a torsor over the Euclidean space of the same dimension, a vector space once the origin is fixed, a norm and an inner product, and a smooth manifold, together with a basis and coordinates, length units, the cross product in three dimensions, the relation between spaces of different dimension, and the actions of translations and rotations. Space is also the home of differentiation in a spatial direction, for functions and for distributions, of gradient, divergence and curl, and of the distributions made from functions that are bounded in the appropriate sense.

maps.title: SpaceTime
maps.abstract: Minkowski space-time, for an arbitrary but fixed choice of units and origin and an arbitrary spatial dimension, is a Lorentz vector: a point is its time and space coordinates taken together, and the Lorentz group acts on it. Around it sit the coordinate maps, the projections onto space and onto time and the equivalence with their product, the measure-space structure that integration over space-time needs, including the splitting of such an integral into an integral over time of an integral over space, differentiation along a coordinate for functions and for distributions, and the slicing of either at a fixed instant.

maps.title: Time
maps.abstract: An instant of time is modelled by a single real number, read against an arbitrary but fixed choice of unit and orientation, so that a statement about time has to hold whichever unit and whichever direction of time is picked. Instants form an affine space over the reals with no distinguished present moment; choosing the implicit origin turns it into the one-dimensional real inner-product space that non-relativistic physics usually works with, carrying the norm, the inner product, the order and the volume measure. On top of this sit the derivative of a function of time, for targets that are normed spaces and for targets that are manifolds, time as a bare oriented manifold, and the choices of time unit, from seconds up to weeks.

maps.title: TimeAndSpace
maps.abstract: Euclidean space-time, the arena of non-relativistic physics, is an instant of time together with a point of d-dimensional space, and nothing more: in the non-relativistic setting no symmetry the theory respects mixes the two factors, so the product is the whole story. It has projections onto the two factors that do not increase distances, an action of the Euclidean group on its points and on the Schwartz maps out of it, and time and space derivatives that commute, together with the characterisation of the functions that are constant in one of the two directions.

maps.title: Canonical ensemble
maps.abstract: A canonical ensemble describes a system in thermal equilibrium with a heat bath at a fixed temperature. Its data is a measurable type of microstates, an energy function on them, and the semi-classical bookkeeping (the number of degrees of freedom and the phase-space unit) needed to turn thermodynamic quantities into dimensionless ones. The treatment is measure-theoretic, so that discrete and continuous models are handled uniformly: the partition function is an integral, which becomes a finite sum when the microstates are finitely many. On that footing the Boltzmann and probability measures, the mean energy, the entropies and the Helmholtz free energy are tied together by the free energy as energy minus temperature times entropy, the mean energy as a derivative of the logarithm of the partition function, and the fluctuation–dissipation theorem relating the heat capacity to the variance of the energy; ensembles also compose, with independent systems adding and a system being copied or transported along a measurable equivalence.

maps.title: Temperature
maps.abstract: Temperature is measured from absolute zero and is nonnegative, which excludes the negative absolute temperatures a system with a bounded energy spectrum can carry. A choice of scale is a choice of how large one degree is, and nothing more, so two such choices differ by a positive ratio, and kelvin is the scale from which the others are obtained by rescaling. In statistical mechanics the quantity that actually appears is the inverse temperature, the reciprocal of the temperature weighted by the Boltzmann constant, which multiplies an energy in a Boltzmann factor; on positive temperatures the correspondence is an order-reversing bijection onto the positive inverse temperatures, so a hot system is one with a small inverse temperature, and sending the inverse temperature to infinity drives the temperature to absolute zero. Thermodynamic quantities are differentiated with respect to one or the other of these variables, so the change of variable between them is smooth at positive temperature, and a derivative in one variable determines the derivative in the other.

maps.title: Units
maps.abstract: Every physical quantity has a dimension: a rational power of each base dimension, recording how the numerical value of the quantity changes when the unit of each base quantity is changed. Dimensions multiply by adding exponents and invert by negating them, so they form a commutative group with a rational power operation. Two sets of base dimensions are in use: the LTMCT set of length, time, mass, charge and temperature, over which the typed unit layer and the named derived quantities are built, and the seven base quantities of the International System of Quantities (ISQ), in which charge is derived as current times time; the two are related by a faithful inclusion and a reduction. A unit system fixes one unit for each base quantity, and changing unit system multiplies a quantity of dimension d by a positive factor that is multiplicative in d, equal to one when the two systems agree and composes along a chain, so the value of a quantity in one system determines its value in every other. A value carrying a dimension inherits the additive, order and scalar structure of its underlying type, and a statement is dimensionally correct when its truth does not depend on the unit system in which it is written, which is the formal content of dimensional analysis.
